newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Thousands said to flee major Angolan army attack.
newsitem.headline: Thousands said to flee major Angolan army attack.

text.p: Angolan troops have overrun the diamond-rich northeast, driving thousands of civilians from areas held by the former rebel UNITA movement in the biggest military offensive in Angola for two years, military and diplomatic sources said on Thursday.
The action, threatening a fragile peace process sponsored by the United Nations and backed by the United States, follows the revolution in Zaire, now Congo, which once supported UNITA.

The Angolan government, however, denies it is aimed at UNITA, its rival for control of Angola since the country won independence from Portugal in 1975 and now its uneasy partner in a government of national unity formed last month.

Angolan officials say the operation is aimed at securing the northern border with Congo, which Luanda says is infiltrated by ex-soldiers from Rwanda's former Hutu regime and troops loyal to Zaire's ousted Mobutu Sese Seko.
Angola is widely believed to have provided military and logistical support for the rebel force led by Laurent Kabila which toppled the Mobutu regime two weeks ago.
Mobutu supported UNITA and provided it with rear bases on Zairean territory during Angola's 20-year-long civil war.

A long-time resident of the northeast region said Angolan army used "indiscriminate artillery fire against several towns" targetted in the operation, which had sent thousands of civilians fleeing into government-controlled areas.
"They would pound the towns with artillery then come in with tanks and soldiers. After they cleaned out any resistance they burned almost everything down," he said.

U.N. and UNITA sources say the offensive has been going on for the past two weeks. UNITA has reported dead and wounded civilians, some killed by artillery fire, and the U.N. says the Angolan army has also suffered casualties.
Analysts and diplomats say the army has captured a large chunk of territory and the former rebel force has been pushed into retreat.
Much of the area is off-limits to non-accredited foreigners, and independent confirmation of the reports was not immediately possible.

Officials in the region, reached by telephone on Thursday, said the government offensive seemed to be continuing but has moved further south. One said UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi had accepted defeat in the north and was now worried about an attack on the strategically important UNITA town of Lusamba.
"Savimbi is very worried about Lusamba," said an official close to the peace process. "If the army decides to go after that it will really hurt UNITA."

Savimbi was due to see a U.S. Congressional delegation on Thursday. California Republican Ed Royce, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Sub-committee on Africa, said its four members would try to persuade Savimbi that the peace process was working and that he should end his boycott of the capital, Luanda, where a national unity government was formed in April.
Local sources said civilians fleeing the recent fighting had flocked to the government-held town of Nzaji, near the Zaire (Congo) border.
They said UNITA had tried to recruit Rwandan refugees camped near the border to help resist the government attack.

"After UNITA came and took the men away only the women and children were left and they were in bad shape," said one local resident, who estimated the population of the Rwandan camp near the town of Chicolond at about 4,000.
"The UNITA troops and the men from the camp put up a fight around the town of Maludi, not far from the camp, but they were pretty badly beaten. That camp must have been overrun by now."
